This mod introduces several new mechanics that provides much more depth in combat. This mod does this by introducing: combo streaks, target locking, and 14 unique combat skills.

With this mod installed, you will log into your world with an orb of basic sword technique. The way you acquire/improve sword skills is by finding these orbs then using them. These orbs can be found in dungeon chests as well as a minuscule chance whenever you defeat a mob. From my experience, if you find a good sized abandoned mine you will get majority of the skill unless you are very unlucky. This starting orb allows you to target lock as well as rack up combos. Combos will only count towards the streak when locked on and will reset after the streak is filled. At each combo level, your attack will gain a % damage increase which is determined by your base weapon damage and current combo level. As you find more orbs of basic technique, you will be able to achieve higher combos and thus able to deal more damage.

There are 14 different sword skills that will greatly spice up combat. I will not go into detail with all 14 since they have a great forum page (link later) as well as an in game manual that is defaulted to the 'p' key. My favorite skill in this mod is the sword beam skill that allows a short/mid range attack using the sword. This is very handy against creepers. One key aspect to note is that every skill exhausts the player, some a lot more than others, so care must be taken in to watch your hunger bar before, during, and after combat with skills. Many skills have a huge benefit associate with them but with this great benefit also comes consequences. This is done to make sure this mod does not make any skill overpowered.

Jim Butcher. Both the Codex Alera and the Dresden series are fantastic.
I've heard Dresden recommended before; why does it stand out to you as a great series?

The thing Butcher does better is keep his characters on task and put together a satisfying ending. I love the complex storylines and vast worlds of epic series, but I hate it when they seem to wander around aimlessly and take forever to get anything done. The Dresden series has complexity, but it also has a solid ending in each book. Sure, some issues carry over to the next novel, but you know something was accomplished.

It helps that Butcher writes like a writer, plots like a gamemaster and thinks like a geek.

I'm not usually a fan of books written in first person, but the main character here is funny and engaging. His internal monologuing is both humorous and internally consistent to the main conceit of the series, that being each book is the notes and thoughts the main character, a Private Investigator who is also a wizard, is recording in the course of his most memorable cases. The author has laid out a metaplot, villains and allies that change and grow as the main character does. this makes a rich world that is very entertaining and very re-readable. Additionally, Jim Butcher has clearly laid out the ending of the series and builds toward it with each book without letting that build-up run over the story of the book it is in. Finally, Butcher is a writing machine. He puts out two books a year pretty regularly. Usually one Dresden and one other series. There is a slightly longer lag now that the series is becoming mature, but only 18 months between books is very doable.

It feels a little cliche to say it but the Drizzt series by R. A. Salvatore. Although I haven't finished it yet, it's an easy series to read and doesn't take much thought. Unlike Game of Thrones where every minor character will either be king or dead or both three books later.
The fighting is incredibly well written and detailed. Every time Drizzt whips out his scimitars I get an erection.
R. A. Salvatore is a gamer and his fiction shows it. If you like playing D&D then you should like R. A. Salvatore.
Malazan Book of the Fallen is my fav epic fantasy series and the Dresden Files my favorite urban fantasy.
Epic is pretty much what I'm looking for; have you read the Wheel of Time series? If so, how do you think they compare?
Malazan is much darker and had predominantly gray characters. WoT, on the other hand, was pretty much the last time the good old farmboy-becomes-hero trope was done seriously and on an epic scale.

The Mercedes Lackey Valdemar series is quite enjoyable, if relatively light reading. I go back to them from time to time. They're technically broken up into various trilogies for easy sectioning. I'd also like to suggest Raymond E. Feist's Midkemia books as well. They're also broken up.

Dune - Frank Herbert. Hands down my favourite scifi series. God Emperor I absolutely hated first time, now its my favourite book of the series.

Riverworld - P J Farmer. Really good concept. Don't watch any of the miniseries they are all abominations. Read and enjoy the books.

Wheel of Time. Be prepared to lose months of your time finishing the books, its a long read but well worth it.

The First Law Trilogy - Joe Abercrombie. This was just what I needed when I finished The Wheel of Time and I had a massive void in my life.

Shattered Sea series - Joe Abercrombie. It took a little while to get into but I really started enjoying it. Loved the first 2 books, third is next on my list when I finish my current series.

The Demon Cycle - Peter V Brett. I'm on book 4 at the moment and have enjoyed the fantasy concept of this series so far.
I've gone through wheel of time a couple of times, and I really like the first couple of Dune books (the only ones I've read). I'll have to check out some of these others.

Jack Vance's Gaean Reach stories. A set of stand alone novels that become greater than their parts. World building, hah! Jack Vance builds an entire section of the galaxy, the Gaean Reach. Some of the best SF ever written.
Steven R Donaldson's series like The Chronicles Of Thomas Covenant or The Real Story are fast paced and readable with plenty of terrible stuff thrown in.

The Book of the New Sun by Gene Wolfe - probably my favorite series in any genre. It's a blend of both fantasy and science fiction, in a sense - taking place on a far future Earth on which our current age is little more than dim myth, and in a civilization that's in the depths of a superstitious dark age.

The Gormenghast Trilogy by Mervyn Peake - this is only sort of fantasy, insofar as it takes place in an enormous, isolated castle. It's wonderfully written and includes some of the most unique and vivid characters I've ever seen anywhere.

The Chronicles of Amber by Roger Zelazny - a sprawling and dimension-spanning series centering around the adventures and intrigues of a mostly dysfunctional family of essentially god-like beings.

The Dancers at the End of Time by Michael Moorcock - a wonderful trilogy set, literally, at the end of time - on an Earth populated by a handful of thoroughly decadent and charmingly ignorant all-powerful immortals.

Saga of Pliocene Exile by Julian May - a tremendously detailed fantasy/science fiction epic about an advanced civilization on prehistoric Earth.

I already mentioned The Dresden Files below, but I will also highly recommend Memory, Sorrow and Thorn by Tad Williams. Others here mentioned his Otherland series, which was good, but a little hard-to-describe, both to others and in terms of grappling with it as you read it. Memory, Sorrow and Thorn is a more traditional High Fantasy series.

For alternate history buff, I'd recommended The Belisarius Series by Eric Flint and David Drake. Set in the height of the Byzantine empire, machine from the far future start a world war between Rome and India.

Another Alternate History series I enjoy is Taylor Anderson's The Destroyermen. I will admit a bit of bias toward the Naval tradition, so this one may not be for everyone, but for folk who enjoy strong naval yarns and battles against terrible odds with likable characters, then give this series a try.

John DeChancie's Starrigger trilogy is a little obscure and kinda funky, but you can't beat the notion of "Truckers on a highway to the end of the Universe" as a fun idea. The books themselves read fast and are fluffy and fun.

A more pure Sci-Fi series that is a good read is Fredrick Pohl's Heechee Series. Humans use found alien tech to explore the universe as best they can.

For Fantasy, David Eddings writes a damn fine series. Over and over. Not a knock, entirely, his books are good reads.

I'd also recommend James P. Hogan's Giants Series set through out the solar system, these books are a first contact/thriller sci-fi series that are good reads.

Raymond Feist's Riftwar Series is a really good fantasy interplanetary war series.

For alternate history buff, I'd recommended The Belisarius Series by Eric Flint and David Drake. Set in the height of the Byzantine empire, machine from the far future start a world war between Rome and India.

Not really a fan of alt-history (apart from the fictional setting of Space 1889), but Harry Turtledove's Videssos Cycle (The Misplaced Legion, An Emperor for the Legion, Legion for Videssos, Swords of the Legion) have an early Imperial / Marian legion (well, 3 maniples worth) of Roman soldiers in a world where magic exists ....
